newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Roche profits rise in line with forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Roche profits rise in line with forecasts.

text.p: Roche Holding AG, the Swiss pharmaceuticals group, said on Monday that net profit rose 16 percent in 1996 to 3.90 billion Swiss francs ($2.7 billion), a result in line with market expectations.
Roche, less than half the size of the newly-created mega drugs group Novartis AG, also raised its dividend by 17 percent to 75 francs per share from 1995's 64 francs.
"The profit figure is very close to what I expected and the dividend is spot on," said Genghis Lloyd-Harris of Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB), investment arm of the Credit Suisse Group.
Roche already reported in January that its 1996 sales rose 11 percent to 15.96 billion francs and it did not provide any further clues to its operating or significant financial results.
"We still don't have enough information for a qualified analysis of 1996 results," said analyst Birgit Kulhoff of UBS.
The consensus forecast for Roche had called for a 1996 profit rise of some 17.6 percent to 3.97 billion francs.
Despite the lack of detailed financial information, analysts confirmed their bullish views on Roche, based on its past record of high earnings and a pipeline of promising new drugs.
"Roche is still on track," said Mark Becker of J.P. Morgan, speculating that operating profits and margins were likely to have strengthened in 1996.

Roche did not make any forecast for the current year, but analysts expect another solid rise in earnings as new products come on stream. Roche has some 23 new products in the latter stages of clinical trials and some of these are coming to market in 1997.
Among the drugs that have the potential to be blockbusters, Roche will be introducing Posicor, a cardio-vascular drug, Xenical for obesity and Tasmar for Parkinson's disease.
Full financial results for Roche, including a breakdown of operational and financial income, will be provided in mid-April.
Apart from the bottom-line result, Roche said 1996 capital spending rose to 1.6 billion francs from 1.5 billion while group research and development expenditure rose to 2.4 billion from 2.3 billion.
Spending on research and development in the important pharmaceuticals division rose to 2.1 billion from 1.96 billion, or 20 percent of the division's sales.
Like most other drug companies worldwide, Roche also continues to cut its workforce amidst rising profits and employed 48,972 people at the end of 1996, down from 50,497.
Roche also continued to pick Britain's Glaxo Wellcome Plc for brain power by hiring Jonathan Knowles to succeed Juergen Drews as head of its group pharmaceutical research.
In 1995 Franz Humer, previously chief operating officer at Glaxo, became head of Roche's pharmaceuticals division.

Drews, who has been head of Roche research since 1986 and instrumental in making the company one of the top innovators in the industry, is retiring both as head of research and from the executive committee.
Knowles has been director of the Glaxo Institute for Molecular Biology in Geneva since 1989 in addition to heading up research for Glaxo Wellcome Europe.
He will join Roche on September 1, and effective January 1, 1998, he will assume responsibility for group pharmaceutical research as a member of the executive committee.
-- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340 ($ = 1.462 Swiss Francs)
